p: The system requirements review passed with four actions, and HEARTH's baseline was set at three hundred and ninety six requirements.
Helen said it was the first set she'd read that sounded like it had met a crew.
Wes had three changes waiting for Friday's board: a hatch handle on both sides, seat track down both sides of the aisle, and every harness run overhead.
Then Nadia found his revision C hatch drawing on the plotter, dated three days before anyone decided the changes, with all three drawn in and the aisle eleven centimeters narrower than the tape.
Her father had texted that she'd missed Sunday with Callie, so Sunday at noon is in her calendar now with an alarm on it.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He drew his changes before the board decided them.
Jun Takeda. Keeps the model. He presented the trace at the review.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead, now planning how to check every line.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She shook Nadia's hand after the review.
Odette. Safety engineer. She asked what has to break for the hatch to open.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She asked for sixty seconds, knowing better.
Chapter four. Shape of the System.

Revision C had come off Wes's plotter three days before the SRR. On Friday of week six Nadia took it to his desk at a quarter past eight, before the board met, before she could talk herself out of it. She'd practiced the first sentence in the hallway. You drew this before anyone decided it.

Wes's desk was the one by the windows. He had a breakfast burrito going and the structures schedule up on both screens. His paperweight was a test coupon from a pressure vessel, bent in half on purpose.
She spread the sheet over his keyboard. This is really clean work, she said.
So that was what came out instead.
It's a hatch, Wes said. I've drawn forty.
The aisle's eleven centimeters narrower than the tape.
Seat track down both sides. Crew needs somewhere to clip stuff that isn't the floor. He found note eight with a finger that had salsa on it. Every cargo module had it.
Cargo didn't sleep in there. She didn't say that either. She said, Can we talk about the aisle?

We're talking. There was a photo pinned over his desk of the 2019 cargo module in the test cell, the one that leaked at the hatch seal. Wes had found that leak himself. Everybody at FRO knew the story, mostly from Wes. He'd been right about almost everything since she got here, which made this harder.
Her stomach did its usual thing. The next word was supposed to be no. She was already shopping for a nicer one.
Colleen's Flight Notes: what it does, then where it goes.

Colleen volunteered Saturdays at the air museum at old Lowry, and she met Nadia beside a jet trainer with an access panel off its side. Behind the panel ran a bundle of wire as thick as a wrist, every wire tagged at both ends.
Everybody photographs the cockpit, she said. This is the airplane.

System architecture definition works from the system requirements, and in practice it runs alongside requirements definition, each one shaping the other. Its job is to come up with candidate architectures, pick one or more that best meet the system requirements and the stakeholders' concerns, and describe it in a consistent set of models and views. It takes in the system requirements, the life cycle concepts and scenarios, the constraints, and what's known about the systems around it. It puts out an architecture description: the elements, the interfaces between them, the requirements allocated to each element, and the reasons for the choices. Design definition picks it up next and adds the detail to build or buy each element. System analysis checks the candidates. Integration and verification plan around the interfaces.

An architecture has two halves. The functional architecture says what the system must do, broken into functions and the flows between them, with no hardware named. Many sources call this the logical architecture. The physical architecture says which elements will do it and how they connect. Allocation joins the two: each function, and each requirement, goes to the element or elements responsible, often with derived requirements written for each. Wes drew a good airplane, Colleen said. Now ask him what it's for, one function at a time.

How the exam asks it. Architecture defines elements and interfaces at the system level. Design definition adds the detail to build them. If an answer jumps to detailed design before functions are allocated, it's out of order.

An interface is anywhere two elements exchange something: power, data, heat, fluid, force, or a crew member's hand. Most integration trouble starts at one. An N-squared diagram finds them on purpose. Put the elements on the diagonal. By the usual convention, a mark in an element's row shows what it sends to the element in that column, and a mark in its column shows what it receives. With n elements there are n times one less than n possible one way interfaces, so no pair gets skipped for lack of imagination. Busy rows and columns show the tightly coupled elements. Empty cells are claims too.

Interface management, as a method, means identifying every interface, defining it, controlling it, and verifying that both sides meet it. A definition says what crosses, in what form, at what values, and who owns each side. It lives in interface requirements and an interface control document, or ICD, that both owners agree to. Once it's agreed, the ICD goes under configuration control, so a change takes a change request, an impact assessment, and sign off from both sides.
Two different crews built the front and back of this airplane, Colleen said. The wire works because they agreed on the plug before either one built anything.

How the exam asks it. N-squared: row is output, column is input, and n times one less than n possible cells. A change to an agreed ICD is a configuration management item for both parties, not a quick fix by one.

Colleen climbed into the front seat and pointed at the gauges. Each one showed one thing to the person who needed it. The architecture description standard, ISO 42010, describes architecture the same way. Stakeholders have concerns. A viewpoint sets the conventions for building a kind of view that frames certain concerns: which models, which notation, which rules. A view applies a viewpoint to this system. The architecture description names the stakeholders and their concerns, and holds the viewpoints, the views, and the reasoning behind them. Helen's crew movement view, the safety office's hazard view, and Tiago's test access view should all come from one model so they can't disagree.

In model based systems engineering the model is the main work product and documents come out of it. In SysML, a block definition diagram shows what the system is made of, an internal block diagram shows how the parts connect through ports, and activity, sequence and state diagrams show behavior. A digital thread links the data across the life cycle, from requirements to model to CAD, analysis and test, so a change can be followed. A digital twin is a model of one specific built unit kept in step with data from it. HEARTH won't have a twin until there's hardware. Someone also has to decide which copy of the model is the authoritative one, who can read it, and who can change it. That's information management, and on a model based program the model is what it manages.
How the exam asks it. Viewpoint is the template; view is the product. Concerns belong to stakeholders. Internal block diagram for ports and connections; block definition diagram for hierarchy.
One airplane in a big sky.

This jet was never the system, Colleen said, and patted the panel closed. The system was the jet, the tankers, the radar, the tower, and a thousand people who didn't work for my wing. A system of systems is made of systems that are independent in operation and in management. Each has its own owner, purpose and life cycle, and could run on its own. In a directed one, the whole is built and managed centrally for a set purpose, and the constituents, though they could still run on their own, normally serve that purpose. In an acknowledged one, there are shared goals and a designated manager, but each constituent keeps its own owner and funding. In a collaborative one, the constituents agree to work together with no central authority. A virtual one has neither a central manager nor an agreed central purpose. Halo Station is close to acknowledged: Halo owns the station's rules, and other companies own the modules.

System analysis supplies the data behind technical decisions. You start from the question, pick a level of detail that fits the decision, write down every assumption, and hand the results, with their uncertainty, to whoever has to decide.

Before she left, Colleen asked about Jun. INCOSE's systems engineering competency framework sorts what an engineer needs into core, professional, management, technical and integrating groups, at five levels from awareness through supervised practitioner, practitioner and lead practitioner to expert. Somebody put your name forward once, she said. Your turn.

How the exam asks it. Clues for a system of systems: constituents with their own owners and missions, behavior that only exists across them, and no single owner of everything. Directed, acknowledged, collaborative, virtual runs from most central control to least.
Wes's three change requests were first on the board's agenda at ten. The drawing had already answered all three.
Structures releases the frame drawings in two weeks, Wes said, or the long lead aluminum slips a month. Amara will tell you the same.
Revision C showed where everything went. What does Nadia say?
A. Let all nine frames go now, and raise the aisle again at the design review.
B. Hold revision C as a candidate until the functions are mapped, and free safe frames.
C. Approve revision C with the aisle width as an owned, dated item for the trade study.
D. Approve revision C as the architecture, and let structure release all nine frames.

She says it in one breath, which isn't how she rehearsed it. Wes looks at her for a while. Which frames. She has them circled already. He releases six of nine that afternoon and writes HOLD on the other three in block letters. Two weeks, he says. Then I want my aisle back.

That's the move. Functional and physical architecture develop together, but the functions come first so the elements answer real needs. Treating a drawing as one candidate keeps it honest, and freeing the parts no open function depends on protects the schedule.

Sunday at noon the alarm she'd set went off, and she made the call she'd promised. Monday she and Jun took the big conference room, the one with the old lighting diagram still ghosted under the whiteboard.

Jun had started a function list over the weekend. It was long, and it read like a parts catalog: air rack functions, thermal functions, power functions. That's how Wes splits up the work, he said. So that's how I split up the functions.
What should a functional architecture be built around?
A. Rebuild the list from what HEARTH must do, with no hardware named.
B. Keep Jun's subsystem lists and add a column for crossing functions.
C. Skip the function list and go straight to the physical boxes.
D. Start from FRO's last cargo module function tree and add a crew branch.

They put five verbs at the top: keep the crew alive, protect them from hazards, house them, connect to the station, support the module for fifteen years. By Wednesday "protect from hazards" has a branch that runs detect fire, warn the crew, stop the air moving, put it out. None of the boxes has a part number. Jun keeps reaching for one and stopping.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. A functional architecture describes what the system does and the flows between functions, without naming hardware. Organizing it by subsystem bakes in the physical answer and hides functions no subsystem owns.
By Thursday Jun had turned the functions and the subsystems into an N-squared diagram, printed on a plotter sheet that covered the conference table.

HEARTH N-squared diagram, draft 1 (excerpt). On the diagonal: Structure, Air rack, Thermal, Power, Avionics, Fire detection, Crew systems, Halo Station.. Across a row: what that element sends. Down a column: what it receives.. Power sends to: air rack, thermal, avionics, fire detection, crew systems.. Air rack sends to: thermal (heat), avionics (status), crew systems (cabin air).. Thermal sends to: air rack (coolant), avionics (coolant), Halo Station (heat).. Halo Station sends to: power (station power), avionics (commands), thermal (radiator loop).. Marked cells: 21 of 56.

Tiago leaned on the table with both hands and tapped the air rack's row. That one's going to be trouble. Every mess I've ever had in a test cell started in a row like that. Wes wanted to know what anybody planned to do with a chessboard.
Jun's N-squared draft has twenty one of fifty six cells marked. What should the team do with them?
A. Turn each mark into an interface with two owners and a definition.
B. Redraw it as a block diagram with arrows for Wes and the reviewers.
C. Mark only the cells where FRO builds both sides of the link.
D. Put the matrix in the review package and walk the reviewers through it.

Twenty one marks become twenty one entries in an interface register, each with two owners and a blank where the definition goes. Only power and thermal have more marks than the air rack, and those two are FRO's own. Tiago circles the air rack's row in pencil and this time doesn't say anything.

Exactly right. An N-squared diagram finds interfaces systematically: each off-diagonal mark is something one element gives another. Turning marks into managed interfaces, and noticing the most coupled elements, is what makes it worth printing.

The next week Jun moved the architecture into the model. Wes came by while an internal block diagram was on the screen: a block for each subsystem, small squares along their edges, and lines running between the squares.
Ports, Jun said. Where things go in and out. Wes looked at Nadia as if the answer had been a dare. How should the model show HEARTH's physical architecture?
A. Keep the architecture in slides that Wes can edit, one per subsystem.
B. Use block definition diagrams and leave the connections to the ICDs.
C. Model every interface down to its connector pins in the block diagrams now.
D. Add internal block diagrams with typed ports under the block breakdown.

Jun types every port: 120 volts DC, coolant at a set flow and temperature, a data link, cabin air. When he joins two ports of different types, the line turns red. He does it once on purpose so Wes can see. Huh, Wes says. It argues back.

That's the move. In SysML a block definition diagram shows what the system is made of, and an internal block diagram shows how the parts connect through ports, with typed flows. Typed ports let the model catch a mismatched interface before the hardware does.
Decision five. Where each one lives.
By the end of week seven they were allocating. Each function went to the element that would perform it, and each got a verification point: the place Tiago would prove it worked.

Detect fire went to the fire detection and suppression subsystem. Tiago asked where he should verify it. Nadia picked the cabin smoke sensor in the main air return above the galley. Galleys were where fires started. Helen's had. And all of the cabin's air came back there to the fans. Tiago could hold a calibrated smoke source under it and watch it alarm. It was testable, and it would pass. In the verification point column she typed cabin smoke sensor, verified by test, and they moved to the next row.
The next row was egress. Hatch, Wes said from the doorway. Hatch is structure. Give it to me.
Each function is going to the element that performs it. How should egress be allocated?
A. Allocate egress to every element it needs, with one owner for all of it.
B. Leave egress unallocated until the trade study settles the layout.
C. Spread egress across the elements and let each owner write a share.
D. Allocate egress to structure as Wes asks, with the hatch as its home.

The egress row becomes four rows, each with a derived requirement traced to the parent. Wes gets the hatch and the aisle. Odette gets the alarm, and crew systems gets the lights. Nadia keeps the whole function, and the parent requirement points at all four.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Allocation assigns functions and requirements to elements. When one function needs several elements, each gets a derived requirement traced to the parent, and somebody still owns the function end to end.

Halo wanted an architecture walkthrough in week eight. Helen wanted to see how a crew moved through the module. The observer from OCSC wanted the hazard controls. Halo's station integrators wanted interfaces. Tiago wanted to know where his test ports would be.
Wes had one answer for all of them. Send them revision C. It's all on there.
Helen, OCSC, the station integrators and Tiago all want different things from the walkthrough. What should FRO show?
A. Send revision C and the N-squared to everyone as one picture.
B. Have each lead build slides for their own audience at the walkthrough.
C. Build each group a view from the model, framed by its concerns.
D. Give every group read access to the whole model and let them search it.

Five views, each with its viewpoint written down: crew movement, hazard controls, station interfaces, test access, and a structural view for Wes, which he didn't ask for and reads first. They all come from one model, so when the hatch moves, it moves in all five.

Exactly right. Under ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, stakeholders have concerns, a viewpoint sets out how to build a view that frames them, and a view applies it to this system. Views drawn from one model stay consistent.
Halo's interface working group would meet for the first time at the end of week eight, and Amara wanted FRO's interface list presented. You present it, she told Nadia. Jun can run the slides.

Jun had built every line of that list. He'd presented the trace at the SRR, from notes, to people who'd already read it. He'd never had to answer a customer who hadn't. He was already nodding at Amara.
Amara wants FRO's interface list presented at Halo's first working group. Who should present it, and how?
A. Present it herself, and ask Amara to send Jun to a modeling course.
B. Do a dry run with Jun and have him present with her beside him.
C. Present the interface list herself at the working group as Amara asked.
D. Let Jun present it on his own, as the person who built the list.

They run it twice on Thursday. The second time, Jun stops reading the slides. Afterward they open the competency framework Colleen sent, and Jun picks two to work on, interfaces and communication. He rates himself a supervised practitioner on both. Nadia tells him he's underselling the first one.

That's the move. Human resource management develops people's competencies on the project, not just assigns them. A supported stretch, prepared and backed up, and a plan against a competency framework grow the person and the program.
Decision eight. One box of six.

Halo's station integration lead opened the working group with one slide. HEARTH was a small box on it, one of six: the core module, the power and radiator truss, the robotic arm, a lab module another company was building, the visiting crew vehicles, and the ground. Each box had a different owner and a different contract.
We don't build any of these, the lead said. We own the station. Wes leaned over to Nadia. Then who's in charge of ours?
On Halo's slide, HEARTH sits beside five other boxes with their own owners. How should FRO work within that?
A. Follow Halo's interface spec to the letter and decide the rest at FRO.
B. Ask Halo to take design authority over HEARTH for the station.
C. Get HEARTH right on its own terms for Halo to fit in later.
D. Treat HEARTH as one constituent bound by the station's shared rules.

Nadia writes it at the top of the interface list: FRO owns HEARTH, Halo owns the station's rules and how the station behaves as a whole, and disagreements go to the working group in writing. The integration lead reads it and asks if Halo can borrow the sentence.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. In a system of systems, each constituent keeps its own owner and management. The SoS authority sets the shared rules and owns the behavior that only exists across constituents. Know where your authority ends.

At the start of week nine Halo issued a station change. Every module would use the station's caution and warning tones and the station's panel, so a crew member heard one alarm language wherever they were. HEARTH's own alarm, which Helen had chosen to be heard in every quarter, was out.
Odette brought the page to Nadia's desk. One alarm language in every module. That's the right rule, she said. We picked ours so you'd hear it through a curtain, though. I want theirs to do the same.
Halo's station change replaces HEARTH's own alarm with the station's tones. How should FRO respond?
A. Adopt the station tones as issued and log the audibility question.
B. Keep HEARTH's own alarm, which Helen chose for every quarter.
C. Adopt the station alarm and check it's heard in every bunk.
D. Hold the change until Halo issues a paid contract modification.

Jun traces the change: the alarm function, two interfaces and the audibility requirement. The station tones run a little quieter than HEARTH's. Nadia writes it up, and Halo agrees to a louder speaker in HEARTH inside the station's rules. Helen signs off on the speaker herself.

Exactly right. Station-wide behavior belongs to the SoS authority, so HEARTH follows the shared rule. As a constituent, its job is to assess the impact on its own requirements and settle conflicts formally, not ignore the rule or quietly lose a need.

Tiago caught Nadia in the high bay with a draft test procedure in one hand. Every number in here I typed from the requirements PDF. If one changes, I won't know. Wes's CAD won't know either. The model knows, and that's it.

Jun had ideas about that, and he had them at length. His roommate wrote discharge forecasting software at Halcyon AI, across town, and Jun liked to point out that his own model only had to predict a hatch.
Tiago types every number in his procedures from the requirements PDF. What should tie the data together?
A. Export a weekly snapshot of the model for everyone's copies.
B. Wait for CDR, when the design is stable, to link up all the tools.
C. Link requirements, model, CAD and test steps by ID, interfaces first.
D. Move requirements, the model, CAD and test procedures into one new tool.

Jun and Tiago wire up the first links in a week. Each test step points to the requirement it checks, and each requirement to the model element and the drawing where it lives. Wes changes a hatch dimension on Thursday. By Friday two of Tiago's test steps are flagged. Okay, he says. That's worth something.

That's the move. A digital thread connects authoritative data across the life cycle, so a change can be followed to everything it touches. Starting with the riskiest links gets value early without trying to connect everything at once.

Tamarack's proposal gave one number for the heat the air rack would dump into HEARTH's coolant loop. Jun wanted to know whether the loop could take it in every mode the crew would use. Amara wanted the answer by Friday.
Use their number, she said. It's in a signed proposal. Tiago, passing with a cart, said thermal vacuum testing would settle it for sure in about two years.
Jun asks whether HEARTH's coolant loop can take the air rack's heat. How should the team find out?
A. Order a full computer model of the cabin's heat and airflow first.
B. Run a heat balance mode by mode, writing down each assumption.
C. Wait for thermal vacuum testing to measure the real rack.
D. Check Tamarack's proposal number against the loop's full capacity.

Jun builds a heat balance for each mode in two days: sleep, nominal, exercise, and a hot orbit. The loop holds in all of them except exercise in a hot orbit, where it's tight. At the top of the page he writes: rack heat from Tamarack proposal, not design data. Nadia circles that line.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. System analysis gives decision makers data they can trust: the right question, detail matched to the decision, assumptions and uncertainty stated. Its results feed architecture and design.

Halo sent its interface requirements for the berthing mechanism, station power, data and the radiator loop. The same afternoon Pavel Ruzicka at Tamarack sent an email. Their rack came from the same family they'd flown on the old station, he wrote. It would drop right in, and the details could be sorted out at integration, the way they always had been.
Jun's list had twenty one interfaces. Eleven had a definition both sides had signed.
Pavel says Tamarack's rack will drop right in, with details sorted at integration. How should its interfaces be handled?
A. Use ICDs for the station and a Tamarack datasheet for the rack.
B. Let Tamarack define the rack's interfaces and fit HEARTH to them.
C. Run Halo's interfaces through ICDs and settle Tamarack's on email with Pavel.
D. Bring the rack's interfaces under signed ICDs, the same as the station's.

Halo's integration lead takes the station side. Pavel agrees, sounding a little hurt, to send Tamarack's interface data for an ICD by the end of the week. Every row on the list has two owners and a due date.

Exactly right. Interface management identifies, defines, controls and verifies interfaces, with both sides agreeing to an ICD that goes under configuration control. Supplier interfaces need it as much as outside ones.

At the end of week eight Jun had presented FRO's interface list to Halo's working group, with Nadia in the chair beside him. When Halo's lead asked who owned the rack coolant interface, he answered without looking at her.
On Friday Tamarack's interface data arrived.
It came in on the date Jun had asked for, with Pavel's name at the bottom. Jun loaded it into the model that afternoon.
He gave the rack a block in the model, typed its ports from Pavel's data, and connected them to HEARTH's. Three of the four lines turned red.

HEARTH model, interface check: Tamarack air revitalization rack. Power: rack input 28 V DC. HEARTH distribution 120 V DC. MISMATCH.. Coolant: rack quick disconnects one size smaller than HEARTH's, on the opposite face of the rack. MISMATCH.. Data: rack on a fifteen fifty three bus. HEARTH avionics on Ethernet. MISMATCH.. Structure: rack mounting points. MATCH.
Jun looked at the screen and then at her. It doesn't plug in, he said. Not one of the three.

Wes read the three red lines standing up and didn't say drop right in, though she could see him think it. When you call Pavel, he said, I want to be on the line. I've plugged his racks into things before.
Nadia went to the whiteboard. The 133 was still there in its red box. Under it she wrote RACK: POWER, COOLANT, DATA.
She opened a new email to Pavel and wrote the first line before she could think of a kinder one.
